description_full: Hyatt Hotels Corporation operates as a hospitality company in the United States and internationally. It operates through Management and Franchising, Owned and Leased, and Distribution segments. The company develops, owns, operates, manages, franchises, leases, and licenses a portfolio of properties, consisting of full-service hotels and resorts, select service hotels, and other properties, including timeshare, fractional, and other forms of residential and vacation units. It operates its properties under the Park Hyatt, Alila, Miraval, Impression by Secrets, The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, Andaz, Thompson Hotels, The Standard, Dream Hotels, The StandardX, Breathless Resorts & Spas, JdV by Hyatt, Bunkhouse Hotels, Me and All Hotels, Zoëtry Wellness & Spa Resorts, Hyatt Ziva, Hyatt Zilara, Secrets Resorts & Spas, Dreams Resorts & Spas, Hyatt Vivid Hotels & Resorts, Bahia Principe Hotels & Resorts, Alua Hotels & Resorts, Sunscape Resorts & Spas, Grand Hyatt, Hyatt Regency, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Centric, Hyatt Vacation Club, Hyatt, Caption by Hyatt, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Place, Hyatt House, Hyatt Studios, Hyatt Select, and UrCove brands. The company also offers Homes & Hideaways by World of Hyatt, a short-term vacation rental platform that features direct booking for short-term private home rentals in the United States, as well as distribution and destination management services; and World of Hyatt loyalty program, which allows rewards points to be redeemed for hotel nights and other rewards. It serves corporations; national, state, and regional associations; specialty market accounts, including social, government, military, educational, religious, and fraternal organizations; travel agency and luxury organizations; and a group of individual consumers. It has a long-term strategic loyalty collaboration with Delta Air Lines to add highly sought after benefits for members. Hyatt Hotels Corporation was founded in 1957 and is headquartered in Chicago, Illinois.

financial_summary: Hyatt Hotels Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $17.2B market cap on $7.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.
The business throws off $159M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.8× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 1.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 2.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 3.4% of the shares.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.68x).
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 9% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 11% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.05, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $126.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 61% in the 2020 crash and 33% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $33.53 (margin of safety -450%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 33%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $15.25 to $61.96 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 96.0 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 23.7 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 108.3 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 216% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 0.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 1.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 25 covering analysts target $202 on average, 9% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.1%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.31).
It converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.8x net debt to EBITDA ($813.0M of cash against $4.3B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 1.3x.
The current ratio of 0.75 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.4% over 3 years, 28.0% over 5 years and 5.1% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 31%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 2% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 8%.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (3.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 29, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 87.2% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.4%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (21 sales, net $42.2M sold).
It returns 2.0% a year to shareholders (1.7% in buybacks and 0.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.2% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 36.5% of the float, 7.3 days to cover.
people: With about 50,000 employees, each generates about $142K of revenue, 0.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 4.8% a year.
That works out to $3K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.7M (26x revenue per employee).
